centralObject.name: Judge Kelly’s preliminary injunction keeping CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s White House hard passes in place for the life of the case, under appeal to the D.C. Circuit from 2026-10-14

place.why: It bears on the administration that pulled the passes: the passes and the grounds are restored for the length of the case on a retaliation finding, while the Oval Office and the Air Force One pool stay the President’s and an appeal is noticed.

legislativeVoid.why: No statute governs White House press credentials; the injunction rests on the First Amendment (retaliation, viewpoint discrimination) and Fifth Amendment due process, and the access rules are the White House’s own.
legislativeVoid.standsAgainst: The First and Fifth Amendments and Sherrill v. Knight (D.C. Cir. 1977); the restricted-space line drawn in AP v. Budowich (D.C. Cir. stay, June 2025). Same object family as rdg_oq1spmhz7azt (the 09-24 TRO) and rdg_bcmepstrq2bx (the 09-21 suit).

title: Inside the Gates
prompt: A judge made the passes stick for as long as the case runs. Does the injunction keep the three newsrooms inside, through the appeal?
framing: Late on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly in Washington, a Trump appointee, turned his September 24 restraining order into a preliminary injunction: the White House must keep the hard passes of CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists in place for as long as their suit runs. The President’s September 18 ban had pulled 78 passes. Kelly’s 26-page opinion found the outlets likely to win on First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, and on due process, and rejected national security as the reason, noting the September 18 announcement never mentioned it. On October 14 the government filed notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit, and a White House statement said the outlets could report “from directly outside”. The order reaches the passes and the grounds, not the Oval Office or Air Force One, where CNN and Politico were still kept out of pool slots on October 14.

split.seam: y at the centers: the institutional stations read delivery (fluid A +0.45, B +0.15), the populist stations read a badge without a room (C −0.2, D −0.4). At the rim the sign goes diagonal on holder-trust: A +0.6 and D +0.5 (each trusts its holder: the courts; the President, who keeps the plane) against B −0.55 and C −0.7.
split.rationale: The scalar runs along x, the stated object’s line: a Republican President’s press ban held off by his own appointee. The discourse does not split on x. It splits on whether the gate is the room: Budowich leaves the Oval Office and Air Force One with the President, so the populist stations on both sides read the passes as a hallway. At the rim the D station flips positive by trusting the President to keep what counts, which is anti-valent: it believes the order delivers because the order no longer matters to it. The Diatribe’s left-rim line voices A, the right-rim line voices D.

antiValentRationale: At the rim the right-populist station believes the passes stay and does not mind: the President still picks who gets on the plane. Belief in delivery, not approval.

z.pos: the passes stay restored for the life of the case: the injunction survives the appeal and the three outlets keep working inside the gates
z.neg: the injunction is outlasted: the Circuit stays or reverses it, or the White House keeps the newsrooms out of the rooms that matter, and inside the gates becomes outside the room

fluid.zReason: The opinion rests on viewpoint-discrimination findings from the record, the September 18 post never mentioned national security, and Budowich only shielded restricted spaces, so the passes are on the strongest ground a stay panel could be asked to review.

instrument.holder: Judge Kelly and the D.C. Circuit

fluid.text: Read the 26 pages: a Trump appointee found the ban likely retaliation and said national security was an afterthought the President never raised. Budowich lets the White House close the Oval Office, not the briefing room, so I'd bet the hard passes make it through the appeal. The pool slots are a separate fight, and I won't pretend otherwise.

coalition.zReason: The passes probably hold, but Budowich leaves the President free to empty the injunction by controlling pools and access, so the win is narrower than the celebration around it.
coalition.text: I'm glad the passes stuck, but people on my side are already calling this a total win for the free press, and it isn't one. CNN and Politico were still kept off the Air Force One pool the day after the ruling. I keep noticing the people I agree with cheering the gate and ignoring the room.

denominated.zReason: The courts hold the gate and the courts have kept their orders, Acosta in 2018 and the September TRO, so the passes stay.
denominated.text: Kelly did this in 2018 and the passes stayed. The courts hold the gate, and the courts keep their word.

fluid.zReason: The retaliation finding gets deference on appeal, but the Circuit has already said in Budowich that the President's own spaces aren't a forum, so the passes may survive while access that counts shrinks.
fluid.text: As a matter of law, the passes and the grounds probably survive; a factual finding of viewpoint discrimination from a Republican-appointed judge is hard to stay. But the Circuit already drew the line in Budowich, and the Oval Office and Air Force One are on the President's side of it. So the newsrooms stay on the grounds and he still decides who's in the room.

coalition.zReason: The administration skipped the national security rationale on September 18, which weakens its appeal, and the White House answer is to work around the order through pool control, not to win.
coalition.text: I think the President has real latitude over his own press operation, but this was pled badly; you can't announce a ban one week and find national security weeks later. The people I usually side with are treating 'from directly outside' like a legal argument, and it's a sneer. I don't love that my side wants the win more than the precedent.

denominated.zReason: A district judge is running the White House press office until the Circuit stops him, and that's custody the Circuit will reclaim.
denominated.text: One district judge doesn't get to decide who sits in the President's house. The Circuit took this back in Budowich, and it will again.

fluid.zReason: The order protects building access, but the White House has already moved the news-making into pools and Air Force One, where the order doesn't reach.
fluid.text: Fine, the passes are restored, but on October 14 CNN and Politico were still kept off the pools. A pass to the grounds while the President talks only to friendly outlets on Air Force One is a badge, not access. The injunction keeps them inside the fence and outside the story.

coalition.zReason: The legal win is real on paper, but the order can't force access where the decisions happen, and the appeal lets the White House stall for time.
coalition.text: I'm rooting for the reporters, but people on my side are turning CNN and MS NOW into martyrs, and those same networks never fought for anyone else's access. Seventy-eight journalists lost passes, and the people I march with only learned three brand names. The appeal will drag on while the rooms that matter stay closed.

denominated.zReason: Trump holds the gate, the room and the plane, and a court order on paper doesn't change who opens the door.
denominated.text: His White House said 'from directly outside' the day after losing. He owns the door, and paper doesn't open it.

fluid.zReason: Budowich shows the Circuit backs the President on his own spaces, and the White House already controls the pool, so in practice the outlets end up outside the room.
fluid.text: The judge can hand back the plastic, but the President picks the pool, and he isn't picking CNN. The Circuit already said the Oval Office and Air Force One belong to him. So the passes get them into a hallway, and that's it.

coalition.zReason: The passes probably stay through appeal, but the administration's real lever is the pool, which no order touches.
coalition.text: I'm with the President on this, but I'll admit a Trump judge calling it viewpoint discrimination stings. People on my side are already calling Kelly a RINO, and I don't know if that's an argument or just a reflex. The passes may hold for now; the pool is where the real control is.

denominated.zReason: The President holds the gate that counts, and as long as he picks the room the order can stand without costing him anything.
denominated.text: Let them keep the passes. Trump still decides who gets on the plane, and that's the only gate that counts.

LF.text: I read the 26 pages: a Trump appointee called this viewpoint discrimination, and the hard passes stand on the best ground they’ve had since the ban. The Oval Office was never in it, and I won’t pretend it was.

LC.text: The people I agree with are cheering like the press won everything. CNN and Politico still couldn’t get a pool seat on Air Force One the next day, so what exactly did they win?

LD.text: The courts keep their word. Kelly did it for Acosta in 2018, and he’s doing it again.

RF.text: On the law, the injunction probably survives a stay. The Circuit’s Budowich line covers the Oval Office and the plane, not the passes.

RC.text: Most of the people I vote with think “from directly outside” settles it. It doesn’t: nobody said national security on September 18, and that’s going to hurt on appeal.

RD.text: Let them keep their badges. Trump picks who gets on the plane, and that’s the gate that counts.

blindAuthoring.authorNote: I trust D's denominated sign least: R-0921-1 forces a positive z because the rim trusts the President as holder, and I could only voice it as indifference ('let them keep the passes'), which really means the injunction delivers the gate and nothing else. B's fluid +0.15 is also fragile, since a right-institutional reader could just as easily predict a partial stay on the theory that the President has discretion over his own press operation. The surprise was that the object's own z sits near the institutional centers, while the populist centers stay negative even without the rim rule. The Budowich carve-out turns the 'inside the gates, outside the room' reading into a plain description of the facts, not partisan spin.
